speechtext:
1.	Has an order in council been passed amending section 2 of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees' Provident Fund Act. chapter 5, 19-20 George V, and: if so, on what date, and what is the extent of the amendment?
2.	Under, or by virtue of, the said act or any amendment made thereto, is an employee entitled to receive the difference between his present amount of retirement and the amount he would have received had he remained until the age of 70?
Answer by: Mr. Martini:
1. Pursuant to the provisions of section 2 of chapter 5 of the statutes of Canada, 1929, being an act to further amend the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Fund Act, the following orders in council were passed:
(a)	Order in council P.C. 1447 dated August 7, 1929, closed the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways employees' fund to new entrants and also provided that employees of the Canadian government railways in the service upon or after such closing of the fund who are not members of the fund be subject to the rules and regulations for pension allowances as are or may be in effect from time to time and applicable to Canadian National Railways employees under the Canadian National Railways' pension act.
(b)	Order in council P.C. 1956-29/353 dated March 8, 1956 authorized any employee who on January 1, 1956 is a contributing member of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways employees' provident fund to elect to withdraw from the provident fund and transfer to either part 1 or part 2 of the Canadian National Railways' pension plan under terms and conditions as set out in the said order. The privilege of making such an election expired on December 31, 1956.
(c)	Order in council P.C. 1958-47/1680 dated December 12, 1958, authorized any employee who on January 1, 1959 is a contributing member of the Intercolonial and Prince

Edward Island Railways employees' provident fund to elect to withdraw from the provident fund and transfer to the revised part 2, Canadian National Railways' pension plan under terms and conditions as set out in the said order. This order in council passed to enable contributing members of the provident fund to transfer to the revised Canadian National Railways' pension plan if they desired. The privilege of making such an election expired on December 31, 1959.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs or to the Minister of Transport, arising out of a press release that an exchange of instruments of ratification took place on Friday between Italy and Canada with reference to a bilateral air agreement signed in November, 1959. My question is, why did it take two years to exchange the ratification notes of an agreement signed in 1959, and why is it that Alitalia is given non-stop or onward rights from Montreal to Chicago and from Montreal to Los Angeles, yet no Canadian air carrier has similar rights in the United States?

subtopic: CANADA-ITALY    EXCHANGE OF INSTRUMENTS OF RATIFICATION
speechtext:
I am not in a position to say why it took that much time. I understood that it was the practice that the actual signing of documents in such treaties takes a certain amount of time. This air agreement was signed at the time to provide a certain advantage for Canadian carriers in exchange for certain advantages granted to Italian carriers. Rome is an extremely important air centre and Canada had to offer important advantages in order to get rights there. As my hon. friend knows, the discussions that take place at the time of signing such agreements are of

a give and take nature. In exchange for the advantages Alitalia got, our carriers also secured a very good advantage.

Mr. Chairman, last Friday afternoon I sought certain clarifications with respect to Canada's policy on the cessation of nuclear tests. The minister seemed to indicate that he wished to make a statement. I do not wish to proceed if he now wishes to make a statement. At that time we [Miss LaMarsh.)

were called to order because it was five o'clock. Does the minister wish to comment?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would repeat his question.

The minister will remember that at nearly five o'clock, for purposes of clarification, I had asked certain questions more in the form of a commentary than interrogation, to ascertain the position of the government in the matter of nuclear tests. The minister was about to rise, but then the presiding officer reminded us that it was five o'clock. I have some other observations to make, but I now wish to give the minister an opportunity to speak if he wishes to comment on what I said.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Please proceed.

On Friday I had indicated that the government of the United States had announced its intention to resume nuclear tests notwithstanding the fact that certain governments attending the disarmament conference, including Canada, have publicly indicated their opposition to such tests. I had inquired of the government whether in the representations it had made it had taken into consideration facts about which there has been public comment, namely that the Soviet union has acquired, if not additional power to its deterrent strength, additional information with regard to antimissile missile operations. I indicated that important personalities in the United Kingdom had felt that notwithstanding their earlier views, the United States was now in a stronger position to resume tests because of this declared fact.
I also went on to indicate that I had understood that the government's position as stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs from time to time was that the government was of the view that there should be no resumption of tests whether or not a system of control was agreed on between the two main powers, the Soviet union and the United States. I suggested if that was still the case, as I understood it was, that position was different from some positions now being taken by political groups in the United Kingdom other than those now in office.
Since Friday a further development has taken place. While there were some questions asked on orders of the day, all we are given the opportunity to do under that procedure is to ask the minister certain questions to which he may give a reply, but there is no opportunity of commenting on the reply. It seems to us in this party that in view of the importance of this matter, and in view of the fact that we are about to dissolve, we should have a more definitive statement of the government's position with regard to these tests.

The minister is now reinforced in his view by the assertion made by the Prime Minister a few days ago in Montreal that the government's policy was that there should not be a resumption of tests whether or not an agreement was reached with the Soviet union. The positions of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs on that point are identical. Is that the position of the government? If it is we are entitled to have it affirmed, particularly in the light of the different view taken by the eight countries whose representatives are attending the Geneva conference, together with Canada and the great powers.
In today's press and in yesterday's United States press we are told that the eight nation neutral bloc is putting forward proposals in order to try to bring about a compromise between the positions taken by the Soviet union and the United States. We are told that the plan of these neutralist nations provides a form of inspection and control somewhat less than the more comprehensive plan originally put forward. Nevertheless, they have put forward a plan for some type of control. The position of Canada with regard to the eight nation bloc is that she has not formally associated herself with those eight nations which propose a system of controls.
What I think the country would like to know from the minister-and I ask this question not for political purposes but for purposes of information-is whether Canada takes the position that there should be no resumption of nuclear tests whether or not an agreement is reached with the Soviet union, or whether or not we have a system of control. Can we not say first of all that we support the position taken by these neutral nations? Surely the government would not be taking an inconsistent position if that stand were taken, and if we assert that there should not be a resumption of tests whether or not controls are agreed on. The minister undoubtedly must have had good reasons for wishing to make representations to the United States alone, as it is reported the government did through the head of our mission in Washington last week or the week previous. I think, however, that the House of Commons and the country are entitled to have from the minister a more detailed statement than we have had from him thus far on this extremely important matter.
Then when the minister is replying I think he ought to give us some indication as to what are the prospects of the disarmament conference. How long is this conference likely to go on? What will be the consequences if the resumption of tests by the government of the United States takes place as indicated by the
Supply-External Affairs President? On the order for motions we had a report from the minister when he returned from Geneva two weeks ago last Friday. However, we have not had the opportunity of an across the floor discussion with regard to what has gone on at the disarmament conference since that time, or indeed since the conference began.
I understand the Prime Minister spoke in Montreal today. While I have not before me the full text of what he said, I understand that the Prime Minister did say that the developments in Geneva were such as not to offer any cause for optimism. The minister has certainly taken issue with that view. I am not quarrelling with the minister. However, before the conference began the minister said that he was optimistic as to the results; and during the conference from time to time, in answer to interrogations put to him by newspaper men, he continued to sound an optimistic note. I always felt that the realities of the situation, however, warranted a tempering of the minister's optimism. While it is desirable that we should pursue relentlessly our objective of comprehensive disarmament or of arms control, we should not be blind to the difficulties involved. It seems to me that the optimism of the minister in this regard is not shared in the appraisal made of the conference to date by the secretary of state for foreign affairs, Mr. Rusk, and the statement of Lord Home following the return of these two gentlemen from the conference in Geneva. I think the minister would serve a useful purpose today if he indicated exactly what his appraisal is of the situation.
Having said that I thought the minister ought to temper his optimism with an appreciation that was realistic, I should not wish to give him the opportunity, which his ingenuity sometimes affords of saying that he is for disarmament, thus giving the impression that only he is for it. Everybody in this house is for disarmament provided we have present the conditions of control that will not prejudice the security of this country or of other countries. However, I believe the minister cannot satisfy the feeling that many people have on this matter if he simply says that he is optimistic and that we must keep negotiating and trying to bring about an agreement on disarmament. Of course we must do that. We applaud the minister fully in his efforts to see to it that there is the fullest discussion and that this present conference exhausts every opportunity of trying to bring about an accord with the Soviet union on disarmament. We applaud that course fully. However, having said that, we are entitled to have
2992	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs from the government a mature statement as to what is really involved and what are the
prospects.
The United States certainly has not given any indication that would warrant the assurance the minister has given, nor has the United Kingdom. The minister has not indicated what is the position of France. A few days ago he said that he hoped that France would return to the conference table. The fact is that France has not returned to the conference table. France is carrying on nuclear testing. The Soviet union has not denied that, in the absence of certain settlements of a political character, it sees no opportunity of reaching an agreement in the field of disarmament.
Is that the situation? If that is the situation, do we now take the position that the best we can get is some form of arms control? It we take that position, what are the possibilities of an agreement on the limited aspect of arms control? On one occasion the minister said that he was not interested in arms control but that what he was interested in was disarmament. I applauded him at the time.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think I ever said that.

If my hon. friend looks back at the records he will find that last session he did say that. I asked him whether it was the policy of the government not to pursue disarmament comprehensively but to recognize that the most we could get was a form of arms control. I refer to arms control based upon the concepts that we have had outlined for us by authorities in the United States such as Kissinger, Otto Kahn and the like. These are matters that I think are of great concern to the minister and to all who are interested in these matters. We would like to feel that we are not simply engaging in an emotional outburst whose objective is not going to be realized. I say again, we believe that we should have disarmament; we believe that we should pursue that course relentlessly.
Some will wonder whether or not Canada is pursuing that course when we refuse to become formally associated-there may be good reasons for not doing so, which the minister will indicate-with those countries in the eight nation neutral bloc which in their effort to break the deadlock between east and west are proposing a modified form of control. It seems to us that Canada, taking the position that there should be no resumption of tests with or without controls, should not have found it difficult to associate itself at the conference with those countries which are trying to bring about some agreement along these lines. These are some of the questions that are in our minds and as to which 

I think we should ask the minister to give further clarification at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I have often been reprimanded for endorsing the attitudes taken by our Secretary of State for External Affairs on international matters. However, I have no apologies to make in this regard. If the New Democratic party must lose the riding of Vancouver Quadra in the interests of world peace, we will do so happily. I endorse the attitude and the approach taken over the years by our Secretary of State for External Affairs, and place them above and beyond all political considerations, and I believe that the bulk of the membership of the party to which I belong will agree with the basic approach I am taking.
I believe that the interests of world peace are paramount at this time, and that in the main the Canadian people, regardless of politics, are very proud of the positions that have been taken publicly not only here but abroad by our Secretary of State for External Affairs on the really important issues that are facing mankind. I fail to understand the continued questioning and the aspersions of doubt cast upon our Secretary of State for External Affairs by the Liberal party. I fail to appreciate what their attitude is on world affairs. It still seems like the old Pearson attitude, one step forward and two steps back.
I have had the very great privilege, one that has been accorded to very few members of parliament, of being attached to the Canadian delegation to the United Nations for the past five years. I believe only the leader of the official opposition has an equal record in this regard. I have noted the growing prestige of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs in the councils of the world. Whether other nations agree or disagree with the opinions he expresses, they welcome this breath of fresh air founded on that basic honesty which is so much needed in the world today.
I listened for some time to the hon. member for Essex East. I failed to note in his remarks any expression of opinion, but I believe that over the years those responsible for the welfare of the world have heard honest expressions of opinion from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This is most refreshing, both to them and to the Canadian people.
At this time I should like to express only one opinion. I am not too sure that the minister is in the proper place at the present time. I think he should be in Geneva, because I feel he could make a useful contribution. When he was last there I was on the point of sending him a telegram to plead with him to remain at the task and not to return to

Canada, because he would serve the interests of Canada and of all mankind more by remaining in Geneva than by returning to the, relatively speaking, rather doubtful political debates in the Canadian House of Commons.
At this time I should like to make a submission to the minister. I do so in all humility, and I also plead a good deal of ignorance. I am not too sure but that the bulk of the leadership in the Canadian civil service are more interested in the return of the Liberal party to office than they are devoted to serving the interests of the nation.
Shame.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is a slur on the civil service. Shame.
Shame.

It may be a slam against the civil service, but I should like to inquire from the minister whether he is convinced that those who represent us in the international field really represent the attitudes and approaches of the minister or whether they represent the former regime. I have had cries of "shame" thrown at me. I accept them realizing the source from which they came. I am making this appeal to the government of the day because the issues are so crucial. I believe that at least 90 per cent of the Canadian people are deeply appreciative of the attitudes taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs both at the United Nations and at other international conferences, and I would hate to think he was receiving anything less than the wholehearted support of all those who represent him in his absence and who advise him when he is present at these international gatherings.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first may I thank the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam for his very kind words in reference to my work as Secretary of State for External Affairs. They are probably a little biased because we both come from the west coast and have been friends for a long time. In any event they are very encouraging. I have had encouraging messages also from hundreds of people in all parts of Canada with regard to my efforts to further the cause of disarmament and to ensure peace. I could not agree more heartily with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam than when he says this question of world peace is all important. It is the one vital issue today, because if we get into a nuclear war there is not going to be any world left. I think it is just that important that the representatives of every country should do their utmost to see that this utter folly of nuclear war does not come to pass.
Supply-External Affairs
The hon. member has made some reference to the officials of my department. May I say that it would have been impossible for a minister to have had finer co-operation than I have had from the foreign service officers and from those in the department who do not come within the foreign service officer grade. These men and women, I have found, are devoted servants of the country. I think they do an excellent job. One of the outstanding diplomats from abroad told me a year or two ago that man for man there was no foreign service in the world to equal that of the Canadian foreign service. In my experience I have found the representatives of no other country to be any better, and I think none of them were as good. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, therefore, should not worry about that particular aspect of our foreign affairs situation.
In so far as the hon. member for Essex East is concerned, he should know, and I am sure he will know eventually, that anyone who was 22 years in opposition and who managed to survive, is not easily discouraged. By the time I have had the privilege of sitting over here watching the hon. member for Essex East across the way for 22 years he will be a lot less ready to give in than he seems to be today on the question of disarmament or on any other question.
The disarmament conference in Geneva is working on three fronts. One is negotiation on a disarmament treaty. The United States do not like to have it called a treaty because they have a problem with congress in connection with treaties. They call it a basic understanding, or some such thing. In any event, the plenary session is working on the terms of the disarmament agreement and some progress is being made. My dispatches this morning indicate a statement from one of the Soviet negotiators that he thought there was real progress being made in the plenary session on this question of a disarmament agreement. The United States and Russia, with quite a lot of prompting from everybody else, have almost reached agreement on the terms of the preamble. Now the main work on the first part of that disarmament treaty is being undertaken.
On the second front an attempt is being made to reach agreement on collateral measures, namely the prohibition of war propaganda. Hon. members will recall that I pointed out that while the disarmament agreement was being considered in the plenary session the group, sitting as a committee of the whole, was going to consider parallel measures which would not necessarily be written into a disarmament agreement. The United States and Russia agreed that the first subject would be war propaganda. Canada

Supply-External Affairs asked that the first subject be outer space, but we did not get our point and we have not got it yet. However, we are still pressing to have outer space considered in that committee. I hope one of these days it will be, because I think it is extremely important to agree on a declaration that outer space will not be used for the launching of weapons of mass destruction. On the question of war propaganda this committee of the whole has had several meetings and has reached agreement on part of a declaration about war propaganda. They have not yet, however, reached complete agreement.
Then on the third front there has been a subcommittee of the three nuclear powers dealing with the question of a nuclear test ban treaty. As yet there has been no agreement. I suggested that some of the eight unaligned nations should be added to that subcommittee of three, but the three nuclear powers would not agree to it. They are carrying on in that subcommittee and reporting regularly to the conference as a whole. The difficulty, as I pointed out, has to do with verification. The United States have said that it will not have any more nuclear tests if agreement can be reached on the question of verification. Russia has said she does not want verification if it involves sending anybody on Russian territory, and all of us have been trying to bridge that gap. Not only the eight unaligned countries but Canada as well have been doing their best. We are one of the four western powers represented at the conference, so we are in a position to talk to the representatives of Britain and the United States. There have been various suggestions made.
The suggestion made today by the eight unaligned countries is one which we hope will be very carefully considered by the three nuclear powers. As yet it has not been rejected, and I think it would have been a great mistake to reject that proposal out of hand. I am very glad that was not done in the conference at Geneva, because if by any chance it brings about a meeting of minds among the three nuclear powers, then certainly the conference will be over a very big hurdle and this may make all the difference between the success and failure of the conference. If a series of nuclear tests is started now no one knows where it will end, and no one knows what the effect will be on the conference itself.
From the start Canada has tried to keep attention focused on the issues that matter. We stipulated seven different fields in which we thought is would be fairly easy to reach agreement between the Russians and the Americans.
Would the minister advise us what is the latest proposal that he hopes will not be dismissed out of hand?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have not got the final details of the proposal, but it involves the use of the national detection facilities of all the nuclear powers and of any other countries which wish to participate, under the control of scientists rather than the military. The idea is to set up a scientific group which would be able to check on blasts. If necessary it would be under centralized control so that scientific teams could be dispatched to find out whether a seismic disturbance had been an atomic blast or an earthquake or had been caused by some other phenomenon. Generally speaking, it is proposed to use the scientists rather than other regular national bodies, and the thinking behind this is that the scientists in the east and the west have co-operated much more fully than other groups in those respective areas.
No one can say whether this proposal will meet the wishes of the Russians, Americans and British but, as I said, it is a proposal that deserves the most careful consideration.
In addition to these three fronts there is another front right outside the disarmament conference, and that is the question of Berlin. While I was in Geneva there were extensive consultations among the foreign ministers of the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union on the problem of Berlin. Many hours were taken up in these discussions, and today in Washington the United States secretary of state begins talks on Berlin with the Soviet ambassador to the United States, these being a continuation of the talks which took place in Geneva. It may be that the first break will come on the question of Berlin, and it may be that there will be an agreement which would involve Berlin and nuclear tests. I do not know, but I think it is hopeful that these talks are proceeding both in Washington and at the disarmament conference in Geneva. Looking back to last September one must realize that at that time nobody was talking and everybody was threatening. It is very clear that the situation today is much more promising than it was at that time.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has suggested that I should have stayed in Geneva, but there is a practical difficulty involved in following such a course. There is not much sense in one foreign minister staying in Geneva. If the others stayed then it would be a different matter, but for one foreign minister to stay would not mean any progress. He would quickly use up any effectiveness he had were he to follow that course. I would have preferred to see all

the foreign ministers stay there until they would reach agreement on something. In fact I think they would have reached it much more quickly than the delegates now remaining there. That is another good argument in favour of having a heads of state meeting in Geneva, but the danger in that is that they might disagree. That would be much worse than if they did not go there because, should they disagree, then that is the optimum in disagreement. However, I am prepared to go back to Geneva the first minute I think it will do any good.
I am afraid I can never cheer up the hon. member for Essex East about the disarmament situation, but I have not been blindly optimistic nor do I ignore the difficulties. I do not suppose any Canadian secretary of state for external affairs ever faced more difficulties on one issue but, though I am not certain what results we will achieve, there is one thing I am sure of and that is that we are going to keep on trying. Nobody will be able to say that the present government did not realize the seriousness of the world situation in 1962, and that it did not do everything it could to bring sanity back into this crazy world.
When one thinks of great nations threatening each other, and that were the threats carried out it would mean practical extinction with the survivors going back to live in trees or like muskrats in mud banks, then one wonders how much sense there is in human beings. However, I do not believe the people of the world want any of this nonsense. They want to be able to live in peace, to bring up their families in peace and let their children make a worth-while contribution in the world. Certainly that is the desire of every Canadian and of those who carry the burden in all nations of the world. For our part we shall do our best to see that they get a chance.

I want to make just one or two brief comments on the speech made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I greatly admired the first part of his speech, in which he expressed a wholehearted and unselfish desire for the success of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, even to the political injury of himself, but I greatly deprecate what he said about the civil service. I shall not say any more about that, as the minister has answered that part of his speech better than anybody else could.
As regards the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East, he seems to fear that perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs is inclined to be unduly optimistic and perhaps even a bit of a visionary. The hon. member is old enough to remember the first world war, and I am sure he remembers what was
Supply-External Affairs said about Lloyd George by one of his colleagues; that he was "the only man among us who never lost heart". Certainly Lloyd George had many faults but his courage made up for them, and of course Sir James Barrie has reminded us that courage is the lovely virtue. Therefore we must be thankful that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is a courageous and hopeful man, and we trust he will go on displaying his courage and optimism. When fighting was the order of the day he was in the front rank, and now when peacemaking is the order of the day he is in the front rank for that too.

I regret, Mr. Chairman, to have contrasted the minister's optimism with what I think is the realistic position. I do hope the hon. member for Greenwood, who has devoted a long life to the study of international problems, appreciates that I was not in any way criticizing the minister's optimism or his fortitude or his patience. What I was trying to do was to get for this parliament an assessment by the minister of the facts involved in the current situation.
We all applaud the minister's patience. We all want disarmament, and I think I can say there is no one in this chamber at this moment who has worked toward that objective as persistently as I have myself. I was a member of the United Nations disarmament commission for three years. I think I know something of the frustration involved in this matter. Let the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and all the rest of us acknowledge the good intentions of the minister as well as the good intentions of the government in the field of disarmament, but let us not for a moment conclude that the realities of the situation are such as to warrant the view that there is any immediate prospect of agreement at Geneva.
This is not borne out by the statements of the foreign ministers of the United States, of the Soviet union or of the United Kingdom. It certainly is not borne out by the head of the disarmament operation in the United States, Mr. John McCloy. Hon. members who wish to indulge in an emotional sort of tribute to the minister might read what Mr. McCloy has to say about this situation. He does not offer the sanguine conclusion that is contained in these panegyrics to my worthy and esteemed friend whose objectives in the field of disarmament we all applaud. We are a parliament representing the nation. We are engaged in the discussion of a very serious problem. We should bring to this matter the maturity of expression which I think it warrants.
Mr. McCloy-and his position in this matter cannot be underestimated-has stated

Supply-External Affairs in a recent issue of Foreign Affairs that there are very strong blocks standing in the way of immediate agreement not only with regard to disarmament but with regard to arms control, which is far removed from disarmament. He points out as contributing factors the failure of the test ban negotiations to which the shifting position of the Soviet union has contributed much. He mentions the disappointing attitude of the non-aligned nations at Belgrade and at the United Nations last fall. Some of these nations are represented in the 17-power discussions in Geneva. He also pointed out that another obstacle is the stated intention of his own government to resume atmosphere testing in the wake of the Soviet tests last fall. Another factor mentioned was the continued Berlin crisis. He might well have added the other unresolved major political problems which at this time divide east and west.
I believe Canada can make a contribution to this discussion, but I do not think we shall make that contribution if we simply go on saying that we are optimistic, that we believe we shall get disarmament at some date and if we unwarrantedly affirm to the people of Canada after these conferences take place and, indeed, concurrently with them, that progress is being made. Of real progress at this moment there is no evidence before us, and I do not think we serve the cause of disarmament by indulging in panegyrics which suggest the contrary to be the case.
I hope no one who follows me will suggest that I am in any way unappreciative of the good intentions of the minister. I am taking what I believe to be a realistic position. I recognize that when the hon. gentleman went to Geneva he had a difficult assignment. I have already indicated that I think he served a useful purpose at that conference by indicating the points of agreement between the Soviet union and the United States in particular. That was a constructive act on the part of the minister. I applaud him for it, as I did on another occasion. But this in itself does not indicate that we have made any progress in the matter.
What is the situation? The minister talks now about the possibility of an agreement on a preamble to what might become a document, a convention perhaps, to distinguish it from a treaty so as to bring it outside the compass of the Senate foreign relations committee or the congress of the United States. Surely, however, this will not mark real progress. Surely we are not going to believe that because we can agree on a form of words which does not have any operational effect, we have succeeded-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is also the first part of a treaty, the key to it.
I would say that is worth while, but it would be nothing more than what the United States and the Soviet union agreed on September 20 last.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes.

They agreed then on a statement of principles, the kind of principles on which agreement is essential if there is to be comprehensive disarmament. The United States and the Soviet union agreed on those principles, and to the extent that an agreement of this kind is helpful, that may be regarded as an achievement. I know, too, that these principles have formed the basis of a United Nations resolution at the general assembly, and I applaud that, too. But all this is far away from anything which could be characterized as an advance in the field of disarmament. When we talk about advances in this field we should think in terms of an agreement on the limitation of forces, or an agreement to destroy nuclear weapons, or an agreement not to use nuclear power for anything but peaceful purposes. That is what we mean by substantial agreement.
I hope the hon. member for Kootenay West, for whom I have the highest regard and who is taking copious notes and whose interest in this matter is well known, is not going to rise again and say that the hon. member for Essex East is expressing a pessimistic note while indulging, on his own part, in a eulogy of the Secretary of State for External Affairs as if the latter had just died.
You are certainly being pessimistic.

I am not a pessimist. I am a realist. I am saying that much as we all wish to achieve disarmament it is wrong to convey the impression that a great deal has been done when in fact little has been achieved, notwithstanding the good intentions of civilized men such as the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We are not making any contribution to disarmament if we convey the wrong impression. I compliment the secretary of state for having taken the initiative he did in striving to indicate the areas of agreement. What the hon. gentleman might well have done is what Mr. McCloy did in this article to which I referred a few moments ago. He might have indicated not only the areas where there was agreement but as well areas where there were common interests, as well as areas where there are divergent interests. I am not going to mention them, but I think those assessments by Mr. McCloy are worth while and deserve careful consideration by all of us who at this time are considering this problem.

There is one point in Mr. McCloy's assessment of what are common interests that I have not heard the minister comment on at any time and which I feel deserves mention at this time. Mr. McCloy says that one of the common interests is the recognition by all parties of the necessity for the prevention of nuclear war by accident, miscalculation or failure of communication in another area of mutual interest. He pointed out that the Soviet union has indicated a growing awareness of the dangers of constantly increasing stockpiles of nuclear weapons and systems for their delivery. This, he indicates, represents a real problem of concern to both the Soviet union and the United States; not only the danger of war by miscalculation but the danger of destruction by the very existence of these constantly increasing stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
If we wanted any inducement for the minister's efforts and the efforts of other people in the field of disarmament we have it more strongly in this fact, as Mr. McCloy pointed out, than in any other. This, of course, is reason for the minister's concern, but it does not alter the fact that despite our concern, aroused and heightened by this circumstance and other facts, there is little evidence that progress is being made in this field at this time. We must work toward this end relentlessly.
I think the minister was right in the view he took about his own attendance at the disarmament conference. One has to judge the effectiveness of a personality at a given moment. I do not know what the circumstances were but I can readily appreciate what the minister said. We now have to have from the minister a statement about the government's policy concerning nuclear testing. Thus far today the minister has not given us a statement in this respect. I would not have pressed for this but for the fact that I have in my hand a Canadian Press story of today's date reporting a statement made by the Prime Minister on Saturday which is a contradiction of what the Prime Minister said a few days ago in Montreal. I believe it is also a contradiction of declared government policy.
I stated my own interpretation of the policy of this government on Friday last when I said, as reported at page 2971 of Hansard:
I am assuming that notwithstanding this situation. the view of the government of Canada is that the United States should not resume tests, whether or not it is able to reach an agreement at Geneva with regard to the resumption of such tests. I understand further that the position of the Canadian government is as stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on a number of occasions. namely that the Canadian government believes that it is not in the interests of the present generation that these tests be resumed, whether or not there is a system of control agreed on.
Supply-External Affairs
That, I believe, is the government's policy. I take it that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because he did not contradict my comment and because he has answered affirmatively on this point before, would agree that what I said is an accurate statement of government policy. I went on to say:
On other occasions I thought the view stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was unequivocal, but that the position taken by the government through the Prime Minister was equivocal. The statement made by the Prime Minister to a gathering last week in Montreal was to the effect that Canada favoured no resumption of tests, whether or not there was an agreement with the Soviet union. Notwithstanding what may have been achieved by the Soviet union as a result of the explosions of last fall, the view of the government of Canada is that there should not be any resumption of tests by the United States.
I hope the hon. member for Kootenay West is listening to this, because he will follow me in this debate and I know of his interest in this vital matter. In other words the Prime Minister has said, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, there should not be a resumption of tests whether or not there is a system of control. That is the position as we understood it on Friday last.
Today's Ottawa Journal carries under the heading "Policed A-Test Ban Must-P.M." the following Canadian Press dispatch:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has endorsed the western view that Russia's word cannot be trusted in a nuclear test ban without international control and inspection.
"Any unpoliced test ban treaty would be dangerous to the survival of the western world", he said.
"It would be a reliance upon the word of the U.S.S.R. without there being means to assure that their undertakings were being carried out."
That is the reported statement of the Prime Minister made on Saturday last. If true, it is in contradiction to the statement made by the Prime Minister a few days ago in Montreal. It is also contradictory to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has continually said is the policy of the government of Canada, namely that this government believes there should be no resumption of tests whether or not there is a system of control agreed on. The Prime Minister stands today, in the face of this statement, in contradiction to the position stated on behalf of the government by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and which was characterized in the words I used in expressing my view of what the government's policy was.
This is a fundamental and important matter. It is the kind of matter about which the various delegations that have been calling on the government and opposition parties have been concerned. This is involved in the great debate in the British Labour party

Supply-External Affairs in England. This is an expression of disagreement with the position taken by Mr. Hugh Gaitskell. The position taken by the Prime Minister as reported today is like the amended statement of Mr. Gaitskell the leader of Labour party in England. The decision to resume tests by the United States now may be based on a military claim arising out of the knowledge the Soviet union may have acquired following detonations of last fall.
I think the minister owes to the house at once a statement explaining this reported statement by the Prime Minister. We are entitled to know from the government if its policy is that there should be no resumption of tests by the United States or by any country whether or not there is an agreed system of control. Is that the policy of the government? We were told it was the policy of the government and it was not denied on Friday last. I am sure it represents the policy of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but it is not the reported policy of the Prime Minister, who has reverted to the position he took in Washington two years ago when he met with General Eisenhower, then president of the United States. They joined in a communique in which both affirmed that there should be a cessation of tests within a system of controls.
Following that communique I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if there was any change in government policy, and I was told that government policy continued to be that the Canadian government was opposed to the resumption of tests with or without controls. While the minister ingeniously sought to explain away the difference between the announced policy and the policy contained in the joint communique, it nevertheless remained for many people to feel that there was a difference of opinion not only between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence but also between the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said we expressed no opinion. We have expressed our opinion. Our opinion is that there should not be a resumption of tests. We did not, however, lay down absolutely the view that we could have an understanding of that kind endlessly without some form of agreement with the Soviet union. The Leader of the Opposition had proposed a moratorium notwithstanding whatever agreement might later have been made with regard to explosions in the atmosphere, in the laboratory or underground.
This is a vital matter, and as I have indicated a conflict of opinion appears to exist.

We are entitled to have now from the Secretary of State for External Affairs a clear and unmistakable statement as to what is the position of the government. Is this later statement as reported in tonight's paper the position of the government of Canada, namely that we cannot accept Russia's word in a nuclear test ban without international control or inspection? I am not saying that is a wrong position. However, I am saying that is not the position which this government has been affirming through its Secretary of State for External Affairs.

I am very sorry I was called out of the chamber for five or ten minutes while the hon. member for Essex East was speaking. However, since my return I have listened with interest to his remarks.
We cannot agree with his suggestion that there has been no progress to date. From our point of view we simply compare the international atmosphere now with the tension that existed some months ago. We believe that even to keep talking is progress in this very dangerous world situation.
There is one thing that can be said, Mr. Chairman, even though the hon. member for Essex East may not agree. We have enjoyed peace during this period. To us that is a measure of progress. Because we believe that time is on our side, as Churchill said to keep talking is the main thing. The situation may be very frustrating and very discouraging on occasion. However, if the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others associated with him at Geneva and other places can keep talking and keep the peace in the meantime, we think time is on our side and that common sense will prevail because of the growing awareness of people in all countries on both sides of the curtain, as you might put it, and the people in Canada particularly that, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said on numerous occasions, war is international suicide.
We all agree on that matter.

We give the secretary of state full credit in this respect for his efforts. I suppose he will reply to the criticisms made by the hon. member for Essex East with respect to the recent statement of the Prime Minister. Actually, however, we are more concerned with the differences of opinion between the policies expressed by the secretary of state and the Minister of National Defence. They appear to represent two points of view.
We are not the only ones who recognize this fact. There are a great many groups in Canada who do so. I can tell you that we are doing all we can to assist the Secretary

of State for External Affairs to prevail and for his view to win the day in the long run. He knows there are large groups of good women in Canada who belong to various parties; I am speaking of the Voice of Women, and we have two or three quite active groups in my own constituency. I have no hesitation in saying that the members of the Voice of Women movement and the members of nuclear disarmament groups, those people have done more than any other organized groups in Canada in the last year to present their views to the Canadian people and to promote concern about world conditions and indicate the willingness of certain people to do something about them.
I think it is quite fair to say that the Liberal party has been a bit shifty with respect to its policies concerning international affairs. We all know that the leader of the official opposition not long ago made statements that indicated a policy of not necessarily nuclear weapons but nuclear weapons if necessary. Then he gave an interview, and he was very clear cut with regard to his policy of no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil.
Will my hon. friend permit a question.
Yes; I wish to be quite fair.

My hon. friend says that in these matters the Liberal party had perhaps shifted its position, and he thereby implied that its general contribution with regard to this problem had been negligible. I am sure my hon. friend has not forgotten that the Leader of the Opposition, who was an exponent of Liberal policy in this field for such a long time, is the only Canadian ever to have been awarded the Nobel peace prize.

Will the hon. member permit me to ask a question for clarification? Would he not think it a fair assumption that the Liberal party themselves announced they had no policy, but that they might have one if an election was called?
I am certainly not going to enter into politics on this matter.

I have every respect for what the Leader of the Opposition has done in this respect. However, my criticism would be that the Liberal party's policy is inclined to be too much on a day to day basis. They have an ear to the ground, and as they comprehend this swelling tide of opposition in Canada to nuclear weapons on Canadian soil, of support for disarmament and so on, they become bolder and they respond to it. As the days go by-and this is not a partisan matter
Supply-External Affairs -I trust their policies will be as clear cut as are the policies of the party for which I am speaking at the present time.
Which party is that?

I do not wish to speak at great length. However, I think this is a proper opportunity to be quite clearcut about this matter in view of certain events which must be faced in the future. I therefore wish to place on record our policies, and to make a few comments as I go along. This policy was designed months ago. We have not shifted our ground. This is what we have to say with respect to international affairs, disarmament and defence:
The New Democratic party believes that the extension of nuclear weapons to any further states and alliances threatens disaster to the world.
I am sure we can all agree on that statement.
It therefore opposes Canada's troops being supplied with such weapons at home or abroad. At present, except for those nations which have independently developed atomic capacity, neither NATO itself nor its members individually possess or control nuclear warheads. Should they do so, Canada must make it clear that it cannot remain in the alliance.
That is in the NATO alliance, if NATO is supplied with nuclear warheads.
To relieve tensions, Canada should press for a demilitarized zone in central Europe and for the simultaneous disbandment of the Warsaw and NATO pacts.
On that policy we stand.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?
Yes.

What would be the position of his party if NATO acquired or if there was an agreement to give NATO the nuclear deterrent? What would be the position of my hon. friend's party with regard to Canadian participation in that alliance?

The resolution passed at our founding convention was to this effect. If Canadian troops in the NATO alliance were supplied with nuclear weapons, we would oppose the continued presence of Canadian troops in that alliance.
In other words you would leave NATO?
We would leave NATO on those grounds.
You would disband the defence of the free world.

To continue:
The rising importance of Latin America and the mutual economic and cultural benefits which

Supply-External Affairs would accrue to all from closer association require that Canada increase and broaden its relationships with the nations of Latin America.
In that respect I think the minister is trying to do his very best. While there are some at this time who are suggesting that we should hasten to join the organization of American states, may I say it is my personal opinion that at this time we are in a position to do the most to promote the development of a state of affairs to the greatest advantage of the greatest number by being in a position to deal with the United States, with the South American countries and with Cuba from possibly a more objective viewpoint than would be the case if we were in the organization of American states at the present time. However, that does not mean to say there will not come a time when it will be possible for Canada to join. I give credit to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and those associated with him. We have taken a very constructive view with respect to Cuba under very difficult circumstances in the last year.
We now come to our disarmament policy:
The revolution in weapons technology makes two facts obvious to reasonable men. First, annihilation is now a physical possibility. Second, there is no known direct defence against nuclear missiles. Policy must be based on these realities.
The more we know of the potentially destructive power of nuclear weapons and the lack of a genuine defence against them, the more that paragraph in our program is emphasized. You have only to read technological and scientific magazines or a recent issue of Maclean's magazine to realize that there are increasingly solid grounds for that point of view.
The New Democratic government will make a general and searching reappraisal of Canada's defence role. Much of the money which Canada now allocates to defence could better be spent on providing such conventional troops and civilian personnel as the United Nations may require, and on aiding underdeveloped countries.
I can say quite frankly that we look forward to the time when we will cease spending between $550 and $600 million on maintaining troops in Europe and will use that money to extend long term credits to the underdeveloped nations of the world so that they may purchase our industrial products, our agricultural products and so on.
It is questionable whether NORAD ever made any significant contribution to the defence of Canada and in any case it has outlived its usefulness.
We are opposed to Canadian participation in NORAD as we have stated on a number of occasions.
Furthermore, there is every danger that the Bomarcs will be equipped with nuclear warheads. The NORAD agreements should therefore be terminated.

That is the point of view of the party-I represent.
The New Democratic party demands an immediate ban on nuclear tests, both to avoid the dangerous effects of fallout and as a first step toward nuclear disarmament. The New Democratic government will propose a treaty to establish a. non-nuclear club of nations pledged not to manufacture, store or permit nuclear weapons on their soil nor to use such weapons at any time.
We quite willingly give credit with regard to the work being done in this direction by the Secretary of State for External Affairs along the lines of the principles outlined in that paragraph. This is the concluding, paragraph on this very important question:
In the nuclear age effective disarmament has become a condition of survival. Canada must play a much more dynamic role in the promotion of universal disarmament.
In that respect I say on behalf of our party that that dynamic role will only be exercised when the government of Canada is willing to get 100 per cent behind the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the advancement of the policies he has advocated in respect of nuclear testing, disarmament, disengagement and so on.
Any agreement on disarmament will require-adequate inspection and control. An independent peace research institute will be established by the-New Democratic government and staffed by nuclear scientists and other experts to give continuous study to the problems involved in disarmament and the underlying tensions which threaten the peace-of the world.
Just before concluding my few brief remarks, I want to say I am conscious of the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs or any single group of persons cannot build up the climate and atmosphere in Canada that are necessary if we are going to have the cessation of all tests, nuclear disarmament and the developments toward peace we are all seeking. Trade union leaders in this country have a responsibility to inform their members of the situation that exists in the world today and they should do so not only at the convention level but at the union local level. Women's organizations have a responsibility, and I say once again that we owe a debt of gratitude to certain women's groups in Canada for the very effective work they have done in directing public attention to these very important questions.
All of us must accept some responsibility. It is very easy to get up and criticize the government but the people of Canada who are working in various organizations across the country must accept their responsibility so that the members of these organizations will understand the seriousness of the world situation and will be willing to study the question and to support constructive and sound proposals to meet the situation that faces mankind at the present time. I am sure

that if responsible leaders in all fields in Canada would accept that responsibility it would not be long before the great majority of Canadians would be willing to accept their personal responsibility for speaking with one voice so that the policies of the government that will represent Canada after the election, whether that government be Conservative, Liberal or New Democratic, will be dynamic and even more fruitful in the councils of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs is going to deal in particular with the reported statement of the Prime Minister, who now says that there cannot be any agreement to the cessation of tests unless there is an adequate system of controls. The statement went on to say that Canada could not accept blindly an undertaking of the Soviet union in this regard.
The minister's position as stated on behalf of the government is that there should not be a resumption of tests whether or not there is an agreement on system of controls. That statement is at variance with the reported statement of the Prime Minister which appears in tonight's Ottawa Journal, and I am asking the minister to explain whether the Prime Minister has been misquoted or whether there has been a change in government policy in the meantime.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member will find that the Prime Minister did not advocate further nuclear tests, and there has been no change in government policy.

My question was not whether the Prime Minister had indicated that there should not be any further nuclear tests. The Prime Minister is reported as having said that there should not be any cessation of tests in the absence of a system of controls because the governments of the west could not accept blindly an assurance given by the Soviet union. That statement is to be contrasted with the statement made by the minister that the policy of the government of Canada is that there should be no resumption of nuclear tests with or without nuclear controls. Those statements are diametrically opposed to one another. Is the Prime Minister stating new government policy or does this reflect once again a statement made by the head of the government in contradiction of his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs; or are we to conclude that the Prime Minister is now agreeing with the position which has been taken by the Minister of National Defence? Are we back again to the position where there is a divided cabinet opinion on a matter of such importance? We
Supply-External Affairs are entitled to have a clear and unequivocal statement from the Secretary of State for External Affairs on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what you got.

While the minister is deciding on the reply he wishes to give the committee in answer to the question raised by the hon. member for Essex East, I should like to draw the minister's attention to a booklet called "News From Cuba" which has been circulated in the mails. Perhaps this would not be out of the ordinary if it were not for the fact that it has been distributed by use of the franking privilege which is extended to embassies in this country, with the result that Canadian taxpayers are picking up the charge for the postage required to distribute propaganda of this kind. I understand from friends of mine in Toronto of various ethnic origins that other embassies representing countries which are in fact Soviet satellites of one kind or another have also been availing themselves of this franking privilege for the purpose of distributing political propaganda through the mails, some of which is quite offensive to Canadian citizens, particularly to some people who are constituents of mine and are also taxpayers.
I think we should hear from the minister with respect to this policy of allowing embassies to send out to Canadian citizens, who in many cases do not wish to receive this material, propaganda praising the communist heaven in their particular parts of the world. The minister should tell us why Canadian taxpayers should be called upon to subsidize this activity by paying for the mailing of this material.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think this is a policy which was adopted by the government of which the hon. member was a member. There has been no change in policy. Embassies are free to distribute material here and Canada is free to distribute material in Russia.

Is it a fact, Mr. Chairman, that we do have a reciprocal posting privilege in Russia? If so, do we take advantage of it and distribute information there which would be beneficial to the people who do not have access to otherwise accurate information about what is going on in other parts of the world?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not know much about the franking privileges in Russia because apparently Canada has never sent out any material in Russia.

Would the minister inquire into this, because unless we do have some reciprocal privilege, it would seem unfair advantage is being taken of the Canadian taxpayer for propaganda purposes.

He made the statement as he went to preside at a Saturday cabinet meeting.

The Ottawa
Journal, and the Ottawa Journal is known as a newspaper which, particularly on the eve of an election, blindly supports this administration or any administration with a similar ideological content. I would not object if the Secretary of State for External Affairs asked for an opportunity to deal with this matter later, but the statement of the Prime Minister calls into question at once the declared policy of the government of Canada in this respect. Just before he went to the disarmament conference in Geneva, Mr. Chairman, in answer to a question which I put to him, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the government continued to affirm as its policy the fact that there should be a cessation of nuclear tests, whether or not there was an agreed system of control. This statement was made without any qualification by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I noted that he had made it on other occasions.
Then, about six days ago the Prime Minister, speaking in Montreal, expressed a view consistent with this statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs as to the policy of the government with regard to this subject. On Friday last I mentioned the fact that


the view of the Prime Minister, as reported in his speech in Montreal, was now in agreement with the view expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. There was no issue taken with my statement of the government's position. I have repeated several times this afternoon that the government's declared policy was that there should be a cessation of tests whether or not a system of controls was agreed upon. This was the statement of government policy, and I have just repeated it.
Now we have a statement attributed to the Prime Minister which contradicts that statement of policy. These matters are now being discussed in Geneva. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been praised for his work at the disarmament conference and no one has sought in any way to fail to appreciate the contribution made by the hon. gentleman or his objectives, with which we are all in agreement. In the face of this statement of objectives, in the face of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs reported he did in Geneva, he cannot sit idly in his seat without explaining this statement by the Prime Minister which is in direct contradiction to the policy which he has affirmed from time to time. It is significant that the statement by the Prime Minister was made just as he was going into a cabinet meeting.
Has government policy in this regard changed as of Saturday last? Was there a cabinet meeting which dealt with this matter? The Prime Minister, according to this report, said that an unpoliced test ban treaty would be dangerous to the survival of the western countries. This is not the position this government has taken, but it has been the position of the United States throughout. It is a position from which this government did not hesitate to dissociate itself. We are discussing these supplementary estimates for external affairs, and this is a matter of vital importance affecting not only our own foreign policy but affecting the attitude Canada takes with regard to the position of its neighbour on the resumption of tests. This statement by the Prime Minister contradicts in every way the statement of policy given to this parliament by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I merely say that the statements the hon. member has been reading do not contradict the policy of the government. Canadian policy remains the same; we are against nuclear weapons tests.
My friend says the policy of the government is against tests, with or without controls; is that the situation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have explained it; we are
against tests, period.

Now, perhaps we are getting the facts. My hon. friend says we are now against the resumption of tests. Formerly, the Secretary of State for External Affairs never hesitated to add, whether or not we had a system of controls.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Do not put words into my mouth.

Does my hon. friend deny he said in this house repeatedly that this government was against the resumption of tests, whether or not a system of controls was agreed upon? This was the position taken by my hon. friend in Geneva as well as in this house. When we come back to a discussion of this matter at a later date, we will have to confront the Secretary of State for External Affairs with his words, in view of the fact that obviously there has been a change in policy now, a change in policy which is announced by the Prime Minister in this statement which he made as he went into a cabinet meeting on Saturday last. If there was a change of policy, one could understand perhaps that there were good reasons for it. Surely, this house is entitled to know those reasons, and that is what we are not getting from the minister at this time.
What is Liberal policy?

The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that this is the policy of the government: we are against tests, period. The Prime Minister is reported to have said on Saturday, we are against test bans unless there are suitable measures for control and inspection. Does the Secretary of State for External Affairs not think there is any contradiction between those two statements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Question.

No, Mr. Chairman. In view of the importance of this matter we shall simply have to be given the opportunity of presenting the minister with the statements that he has made on the subject from time to time and to ascertain from him why there has been a change, if indeed there has been a change, so that he can tell the country and parliament.
There may be good reasons for a change. The minister is in a better position than anyone else to know, because of the post he holds and because of his discussions with certain powers. There may be every justification for the changed position; but we are entitled to have more from the minister than a statement which seeks to suggest that there is no
Supply-External Affairs change in government policy, and that he himself has never affirmed that there should be a cessation of tests whether or not a system of controls was agreed on.
While one of my colleagues is looking up the precise statement, I would invite the minister-
Here is the statement.
No second leader.
Where is your first leader?
This is a matter of very great importance-
You don't like what you read, Paul.

One would not want to make references to the wrong context, but my hon. friend will remember that before he went to Geneva I asked him a specific question on this very subject. He clearly indicated then that there had been no change of policy and that the government was against the resumption of tests whether or not there was any agreement to provide for a system of control. He said that repeatedly during the last year and a half in this house. I say that the Prime Minister, who is here now, contradicted that statement of the secretary of state by his reported statement.
Perhaps the Prime Minister has not seen this statement. I understand he has been in Montreal discussing disarmament and perhaps he can tell us whether he said what he is reported to have said. Here is what the Prime Minister is reported in tonight's Ottawa Journal, at page 7, as having said:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has endorsed the western view that Russia's word cannot be trusted in a nuclear test ban without international control and inspection.
"Any unpoliced test ban treaty would be dangerous to the survival of the western world," he said.
"It would be a reliance upon the word of the U.S.S.R. without there being means to assure that their undertakings were being carried out."
He made the statement as he went to preside at a Saturday cabinet meeting.
The matter under discussion between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself is: that statement of the Prime Minister is inconsistent with the declared policy of the government of Canada.
Not in any way.

Well, all right. The Prime Minister says "not in any way." Perhaps he will explain to us how he can reconcile these words with the repeated declaration of policy by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the Canadian government was opposed to nuclear testing whether or not there was a system of control. How can

Supply-External Affairs my right hon. friend say that there has been no change of policy? How could he say this is consistent with the declaration of the Secretary of State for External Affairs? The two are absolutely contradictory.
Not at all.

On the one hand you cannot say that you do not trust the Soviet union, or you cannot say you must have a system of control and also agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs who said there should not be a resumption of tests whether or not there was an agreed system of control. These two statements stand in contradiction to one another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nonsense.
The Prime Minister may nod his head all he wants but he will stand in condemnation by the Canadian people unless-
Oh, oh.
-unless he explains this away without delay. He has embarrassed his own Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Rubbish.

He has put himself in a position at odds with one of his own ministers; but we all recognize of course that this has not occurred for the first time. The Prime Minister may think this is a laughing matter-
It is the hon. gentleman's interpretation I am laughing at.
I am not interpreting the Prime Minister's statement.

He said:
Any unpoliced test ban treaty would be dangerous to the survival of the western world.

Is that the same as the policy declared by the government of Canada? The Prime Minister nods his head. All I can say is that by that act the Prime Minister has indicated without any doubt he does not accept the appreciation of the importance of this matter, and that lack of appreciation will be noted by the people of Canada.
